603.title: Whatever is born will pass
603.hook: jo upjio so binas hai: whatever is born will perish, today or tomorrow (Salok M9 52, ang 1429)
603.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, including salok fifty-two, at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, often in the days after a death.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: worry about the unexpected, and your line: nothing stays. Did a predictable worry come back, and did you set it down? Today, the next salok goes one step further. Day six hundred three.
screen: `WORRY ABOUT THE UNEXPECTED — NOTHING STAYS.`

segments.voice: A gardener plants tomatoes in May. By August the vines are taller than the fence and the kitchen counter is covered in fruit. By October the first frost comes, and in one night the whole bed goes black. Every gardener knows this is coming. They plant anyway, every spring, and they don't stand at the window in July grieving the frost. They pick, they cook, they give bags of tomatoes to the neighbors. The ending is written into the seed packet. Guru Tegh Bahadur's next salok says the same thing about everything that has ever been born, and then it says what to do with the summer. Today: whatever is born will pass.
screen: `TOMATOES IN MAY.` → `FROST IN OCTOBER.` → `THE ENDING IS IN THE SEED PACKET.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-two, on Ang fourteen twenty-nine, begins: jo upjio so binas hai. Upjio is what has sprung up, been born, been made. Binas is what perishes, comes undone. Whatever sprang up will come undone. Then three short words: paro aaj kai kaal. It falls today, or tomorrow. The Punjabi word kaal can mean tomorrow, and it can also mean time, and death. So the phrase has a shadow in it. Notice the line doesn't say when. It doesn't threaten. It just refuses to pretend. Today or tomorrow: the only open question is the date. The second line is where the salok turns. In paraphrase: Nanak says, sing the praises of the Lord, and let go of all the janjaal. Janjaal is a lovely, tangled word: the snares, the nets, the knots of busyness and attachment we get caught in. Picture a fishing net that's been left in the shed for a year. So the Guru puts two things side by side. Everything passes. Therefore, sing. Not therefore, despair; not therefore, nothing matters. The fact of passing is given as the reason to spend the time well. This is the same pattern the gardener lives by. The frost isn't a reason not to plant. It's the reason to pick the tomatoes now and give some away. In Sikh life, singing the praises means the Name, kirtan, the daily banis. And it shows up in the way Sikhs often speak at a death: quietly, with the words of the Guru Granth Sahib, and with acceptance of hukam, the order of things, sitting right beside the grief.
screen: `UPJIO, BINAS: SPRUNG UP, COME UNDONE.` · `TODAY OR TOMORROW: ONLY THE DATE IS OPEN.` · `JANJAAL: THE TANGLED NET.` · `IT PASSES, SO SING.` · then, large: `TODAY OR TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with that calmly. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Think of one thing you love that is passing: a season of your kids' lives, a friendship as it is right now, your own body at this age. Don't push the thought away, and don't chase it into sadness. Just hold it, the way you'd hold a ripe tomato: gently, because it won't keep. Then think of one way to enjoy it today. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Whatever is born will pass. Jo upjio so binas hai: what sprang up comes undone, today or tomorrow, so sing while it's summer.
screen: `WHATEVER IS BORN WILL PASS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: today or tomorrow. Pick one thing that won't keep, a call, a meal, an hour with someone, and do it today, not tomorrow. Day six hundred three.

604.title: Strength gone, in chains
604.hook: strength is gone, I'm in chains, nothing works; Nanak says, only You are my refuge (Salok M9 53, ang 1429)
604.howItsDone: Sikhs read salok fifty-three as part of the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many turn to it in illness or trouble as a plain cry for the Lord's shelter.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: whatever is born will pass, and your line: today or tomorrow. Did you do one thing today instead of tomorrow? Today the saloks stop speaking about the world and speak about one person, at the end of their strength. Day six hundred four.
screen: `WHATEVER IS BORN WILL PASS — TODAY OR TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: Most of us have had a version of this. The phone has been called, the forms filled out, the advice taken, and the problem is still sitting there. A diagnosis. A job search in its ninth month. A child who won't talk to you. You've tried everything you know how to try, and at some point you hear yourself say, out loud or not: I've got nothing left. It's a strange, bare place. Pride doesn't work there; cleverness doesn't either. Guru Tegh Bahadur wrote a salok from exactly that place, and Sikhs have read it for centuries as the words of a man in a cell. Today: strength gone, in chains.
screen: `EVERYTHING TRIED.` → `I'VE GOT NOTHING LEFT.` → `A SALOK FROM THAT PLACE.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-three, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. In paraphrase: my strength is exhausted, I am bound in chains, and nothing I try works. Nanak says, now You are my shelter, Lord: help me, as You helped the elephant. Three phrases do the work. Bal chhutkio: strength has slipped away. Bandhan pare: the bonds have fallen on me. Kachhoo na hot upaai: no remedy, no plan, nothing works. It's an honest inventory, with nothing dressed up. Then the turn: ab ot. Now, the shelter. Ot is a lovely word. It means a refuge, a support, the thing you lean on, the wall you put your back against. And the salok adds an old picture, gaj, the elephant. Indian tradition tells of an elephant king seized by a crocodile in a lake. He pulled for a long time with all his great strength and lost. Only when he gave up pulling and called on God was he freed. Gurbani mentions this story more than once as a sign of grace for the helpless. Why does this salok matter so much to Sikhs? Because tradition places it in the Guru's last months, when he was imprisoned in Delhi, before his execution in 1675. Many Sikhs hear it as written in real chains. Historians don't know exactly when each salok was composed, so that link is tradition. Either way, the shape is the point. The salok doesn't pretend strength is limitless. It admits the end of strength, and from there it asks. In Sikh thought, that asking isn't failure. It's where the ot, the shelter, finally gets leaned on.
screen: `BAL CHHUTKIO: STRENGTH HAS SLIPPED AWAY.` · `NOTHING WORKS: AN HONEST LIST.` · `OT: THE SHELTER YOU LEAN ON.` · `THE ELEPHANT WHO STOPPED PULLING.` · then, large: `ONLY YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for help where you're stuck. Sit, and bring to mind one place in your life where you've tried everything you know. Say it to yourself as plainly as the salok does: this is what I've tried; this is what isn't working. Then let yourself lean, the way you'd lean back against a wall. If you pray, you can ask God for help in your own words, or say Waheguru. If you don't, think of one person you could ask, and picture asking them. The bell holds the time.
Strength gone. Bal chhutkio, bandhan pare: strength slipped away, the bonds fell on me, and from there, the ot, the shelter.
screen: `STRENGTH GONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: only you. Today, ask for help with one thing you've been carrying alone, from God if you pray, or from one person who could help. Day six hundred four.

605.title: Strength returned
605.hook: strength has come, bonds are broken; tradition hears this as the young Gobind's answer (Salok 54, ang 1429)
605.howItsDone: Sikhs read saloks fifty-three and fifty-four together at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many tell the story of the father's letter and the son's reply when they do.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: strength gone, and your line: only you. Did you ask for help with one thing you'd been carrying alone? Today the very next salok answers yesterday's, almost word for word. Day six hundred five.
screen: `STRENGTH GONE — ONLY YOU.`

segments.voice: Picture a letter arriving from a prison. Inside, a father has written two lines: my strength is gone, I'm in chains, nothing works. Now picture the reply, written by his son, who is about nine years old. Sikh tradition tells exactly this story. It says that Guru Tegh Bahadur, held in Delhi, sent yesterday's salok to Anandpur as a kind of question, and that the young Gobind Rai, who would become Guru Gobind Singh, sent back an answer in the same meter, line for line. Whatever history finally says about how it happened, the two saloks sit next to each other in the Guru Granth Sahib, and they read like a call and a reply. Today: strength returned.
screen: `A LETTER FROM A PRISON.` → `A REPLY FROM A NINE-YEAR-OLD.` → `A CALL AND AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Put them side by side. Salok fifty-three said bal chhutkio: strength has slipped away. Salok fifty-four, on the same Ang, fourteen twenty-nine, says bal hoaa: strength has come. Fifty-three said bandhan pare: the bonds have fallen on me. Fifty-four says bandhan chhute: the bonds are broken. Fifty-three said nothing works. Fifty-four, in paraphrase, says everything is possible. And then the second line: Nanak, all is in Your hands; You alone are the helper. Notice what didn't change. Both saloks end in the same place: God as the help. In fifty-three, the speaker leans on God because his own strength is gone. In fifty-four, the strength is back, and it's still God's. The return of strength doesn't become a reason for pride. That's the quiet lesson in the pair. We tend to pray when things are bad and forget when they're good. These two lines hold both seasons to the same shelter. A word about the history. The salok is printed among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, and scholars differ on who composed it. Many Sikhs follow the tradition that it was the young Gobind's reply; others read it as the ninth Guru's own answer to his own question. The text doesn't settle it. What's certain is what came next in the story Sikhs tell: the father went to his death in Delhi in 1675, and the boy grew up to found the Khalsa. A child who could answer chains with strength returned. That's how the tradition remembers him.
screen: `STRENGTH GONE; STRENGTH COME.` · `BONDS FALLEN; BONDS BROKEN.` · `BOTH END IN THE SAME SHELTER.` · `WHO WROTE IT: SCHOLARS DIFFER.` · then, large: `ALL IS IN YOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage someone stuck. Sit and think of one person you know who is in yesterday's salok right now: worn out, tangled up, nothing working. Picture their face. Then picture what an answer might sound like, the way the reply answered the letter. Not advice, not a lecture. A few words that hand some strength back. Maybe: I'm with you. Maybe: you've got more in you than you think. If you pray, you can hold them in your mind and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Strength returned. Bal hoaa, bandhan chhute: strength has come, the bonds are broken, and it all still rests in God's hands.
screen: `STRENGTH RETURNED — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: all is in your hands. Send the person you pictured a short message today, a few words that hand some strength back. Day six hundred five.

606.title: All companions gone
606.hook: every companion left, none stayed to the end; only the Lord remains (Salok M9 55, ang 1429)
606.howItsDone: Salok fifty-five is read among the closing saloks of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, who stayed with Guru Tegh Bahadur in Delhi.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: strength returned, and your line: all is in your hands. Did you send a few words to someone stuck? Today, a salok about who is still there when the hard part comes. Day six hundred six.
screen: `STRENGTH RETURNED — ALL IS IN YOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: Hospital waiting rooms tell the truth about friendship. At the wedding there were two hundred people. At the birthday, the house was full. Then someone gets a long illness, and by the third month the visitors thin out. Nobody means it. People get busy; they don't know what to say; they assume someone else is going. And the patient notices, quietly, who is still coming on Tuesday afternoons. Guru Tegh Bahadur has a two-line salok about that thinning out. It's one of the starkest lines in his bani. And the story around it holds a surprise. Today: all companions gone.
screen: `TWO HUNDRED AT THE WEDDING.` → `THE VISITORS THIN OUT.` → `WHO STILL COMES ON TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-five, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. In paraphrase: all my companions and friends have left me; no one kept company with me to the end. Nanak says, in this calamity, my one support is the Lord. Sang sakhaa: companions, friends. Sabh taj gae: all have abandoned, all have gone. Kou na nibhio saath: no one saw the companionship through. Nibhaana is a rich Punjabi verb. It means to keep something going to the end: to keep a promise, to keep a friendship, to keep faith when it costs. Then the second line: in this bipat, this disaster, the one tek, the one prop, is the Lord. The salok uses the name Raghunaath, a name for God that Gurbani borrows from the old stories of Rama. This continues the run of saloks we've been reading: Rama gone, nothing stays, strength gone. Now the people go too, and what remains is God. Here is the surprise. Sikh tradition remembers that when Guru Tegh Bahadur was held in Delhi, three Sikhs did stay with him: Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das, and Bhai Dayala. Tradition says they were executed in front of him, before his own death in 1675, and Sikhs remember them by name to this day. So the salok describes the way of the world, and the story honors the rare people who refused to be the way of the world. That's the double edge of the line. It tells the listener where the final support lies. And it quietly asks: when someone you love is in the bipat, will you be the one who nibhaaes, who sees it through?

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be one who stays. Sit, and think of someone in a long hard stretch: an illness, a grief, a divorce, a lonely year. Someone whose visitors may have thinned out. Picture yourself as the Tuesday afternoon visitor, not the crowd at the wedding. What would staying look like this week? A call, a meal dropped off, ten minutes sitting with them. Choose one. If you pray, you can hold them before God and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
All companions gone. Sang sakhaa sabh taj gae: everyone left, and in the bipat, the one prop is the Lord.

607.title: The Name remains
607.hook: naam rahio saadhoo rahio: the Name remains, the holy remain, the Guru remains (Salok M9 56, ang 1429)
607.howItsDone: Salok fifty-six is read near the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many Sikhs hear it at a bhog as the answer to the saloks about passing.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: all companions gone, and your line: he remains. Did you do one staying thing for someone in a hard stretch? After a run of saloks about what goes, today's is about what stays. Day six hundred seven.
screen: `ALL COMPANIONS GONE — HE REMAINS.`

segments.voice: For a week now these saloks have been taking things away. Rama and Ravana, gone. Youth, gone. Strength, gone. Friends, gone. Whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow. If you've been listening closely, you might have wondered whether the ninth Guru was simply very sad. Then you reach salok fifty-six, the second to last, and the whole list turns over. After all that subtraction, he finally names what doesn't go. It's three things, said in one breath, each with the same verb. And then a sting in the tail about how few people notice them. Today: the Name remains.
screen: `A WEEK OF THINGS TAKEN AWAY.` → `THE LIST TURNS OVER.` → `THREE THINGS THAT DON'T GO.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-six, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Naam rahio, saadhoo rahio, rahio gur gobind. Rahio means remained, stayed, abides. The Name remains. The saadhoo, the holy one, the true devotee, remains. The Guru, God, remains. Three things, one verb, like three posts driven into ground that everything else is washing over. Take them one at a time. The Name, naam, is the whole of Sikh devotion in one word: God's presence, remembered and repeated. The saadhoo is the person who lives in that remembrance. Gurbani speaks often of the saadh sangat, the company of such people, and of how their example outlasts them. And gur gobind here isn't the tenth Guru's name: in this line it's God as Guru, the teacher who is also the Lord. The second line is the sting. In paraphrase: Nanak says, in this world, how rare is the one who has repeated the Guru's mantra. So the three things that last are available, and almost nobody picks them up. That's the shape of the whole salok collection. All week the world was a dream, a show, a wall of sand. That wasn't gloom for its own sake. It was clearing the table so you could see what was still on it. Sikhs often hear this salok as the answer to the rest. It's why the saloks can be read at a bhog after a death without being only about death. The person has gone. The Name they lived by, the good they did, and God, remain.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what remains for you. Sit, and let your breath slow. Think back over the things these saloks took away: youth, strength, friends who drifted. Then ask a different question: what has stayed? Maybe a faith, maybe a person who's always been there, maybe a practice, maybe a line like this one. Name one thing, quietly, to yourself. If you pray, you can repeat Waheguru slowly, as one way of picking up what remains. The bell holds the time.
The Name remains. Naam rahio, saadhoo rahio, rahio gur gobind: the Name, the holy, and God as Guru stay when all else goes.

608.title: Held in the heart
608.hook: I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it (Salok M9 57, ang 1429)
608.tomorrow: Saloks at the close of a reading
608.howItsDone: Salok fifty-seven is the last of Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks and is read near the very end of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; many Sikhs know it by heart.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Name remains, and your line: the name remains. What was the one thing you named that has stayed? Today, the last of Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifty-seven saloks. Day six hundred eight.
screen: `THE NAME REMAINS — THE NAME REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Last words get remembered. A grandfather's final sentence gets repeated at every family gathering for thirty years. A letter's last line is the one people copy out and keep in a wallet. Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks end the main body of the Guru Granth Sahib's hymns, and the fifty-seventh, his last, sits only a page from the very end of the book. After all the saloks about passing, about chains, about friends who leave, what does he choose to say last? Not a warning. Not a complaint. A plain statement of what he's holding on to. Today: held in the heart.
screen: `LAST WORDS GET REMEMBERED.` → `THE FIFTY-SEVENTH SALOK.` → `WHAT HE CHOSE TO SAY LAST.`

segments.voice: Salok fifty-seven, Ang fourteen twenty-nine. Raam naam ur mai gahio: I have grasped the Name of the Lord in my heart. Ur is the heart, the chest, the place you'd press a hand to. Gahio is a grip word: seized, held tight, the way you'd hold a rope in a current. Then: jaa kai sam nahee koi. Sam means equal. There is nothing equal to it. Nothing weighs the same. Raam here, as across Gurbani, is a name for the one God who pervades everything, not only the hero of the Ramayana. The second line, in paraphrase: remembering it, every trouble is erased, and the sight of You is granted. Sankat is a crisis, a tight spot. Daras is the sight of the beloved, the glimpse of God. Look at how the collection has moved. It started with the world as a dream and a wall of sand. It went through strength gone, chains, friends gone. Then the turn: the Name remains. And now the last word is personal: I have held it. Not the Name exists somewhere, but it is in my heart, gripped tight. Sikhs often hear the whole set as the Guru's testimony from the end of his life, and this as its final line. Remember that tradition places these saloks near his martyrdom in Delhi in 1675. If that's right, this is a man who was about to lose everything the world can take, saying that the one thing he held couldn't be taken. Nothing equals it. Whatever the date of composition, that's how Sikhs have read it for centuries.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one line in your heart. Choose one short line from the past few weeks, one that stayed with you: nothing stays, today or tomorrow, the name remains. Or a single word, like Waheguru. Put a hand on your chest if you like. Say the line silently on each out-breath, gently, like holding a rope without strain. When your mind wanders, come back to the line. If you pray, the line can be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Held in the heart. Raam naam ur mai gahio: the Name gripped in the heart, and jaa kai sam nahee koi, nothing equals it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: held in the heart, and your line: nothing equals it. Did your line come back in a tight spot? This week we read saloks fifty-two to fifty-seven: whatever is born will pass, strength gone, strength returned, all companions gone, the Name remains, held in the heart. Today: where Sikhs hear them. Day six hundred nine.
screen: `HELD IN THE HEART — NOTHING EQUALS IT.`

segments.voice: A living room has been cleared of furniture. White sheets cover the floor. At one end, on a raised platform under a canopy, the Guru Granth Sahib lies open, and for several days, in shifts, family and friends have been reading it aloud from the first page to the last. A grandfather died ten days ago. Today is the last day of the reading. The house is full; someone is stirring a huge pot of karah prashad in the kitchen. And as the reader nears the end of more than fourteen hundred pages, the words that fill the room are the ones we've spent this month with. Today: saloks at the close of a reading.
screen: `WHITE SHEETS ON THE FLOOR.` → `A READING, FIRST PAGE TO LAST.` → `THE LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: A complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is called a path. An akhand path runs without stopping, reader after reader, for about forty-eight hours. A sahaj path goes at an easier pace, over days or weeks. Either way, the reading ends with a ceremony called the bhog: the completion. And because the book has its order, every complete reading ends the same way. Near the very end come Guru Tegh Bahadur's fifty-seven saloks, then Guru Arjan's short Mundavani, the seal, and a last salok of his. Some sangats also read the Raagmala; Sikhs differ on that, and the Sikh code of conduct leaves it to local custom. Then the Anand Sahib is sung, the Ardas is said, a hukamnama, the day's word, is read, and karah prashad is shared. So Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are what the room hears just before a reading closes. Many families hold a sahaj path after a death, timed so the bhog falls on the day of the final prayers. Think about what that means. The grieving family sits and hears: whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow. All companions go. And then: the Name remains. The holy remain. I have held the Name in my heart; nothing equals it. The words were not written as funeral texts. They come at the end because of where they sit in the book. But it's hard to imagine better words for that room. They don't pretend the grandfather isn't gone. They name the passing out loud, and then they name what stays.
screen: `A PATH: THE WHOLE GRANTH, READ ALOUD.` · `THE BHOG: THE COMPLETION.` · `HIS SALOKS COME NEAR THE END.` · `THE ROOM HEARS PASSING, THEN WHAT STAYS.` · then, large: `READ FOR THE DEPARTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read three saloks for someone missed. Think of someone who has died, close or not so close: a grandparent, a friend, a teacher. Let their face come. Then, slowly, say to yourself three of the lines we've learned: whatever is born will pass, today or tomorrow. The Name remains. Nothing equals it. Pause after each one. You're not explaining anything; you're keeping them company with the words. If you pray, you can end with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Saloks at the close of a reading. Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks come just before the bhog, so a grieving room hears both the passing and what stays.
